span.label: mechanism
span.quote: The results of both experiments support a retrieval model involving a dependence between separate successive decisions about whether each of the two strings is a word

span.quote: By varying the degree of association between the words, we then hoped it would be possible to test for a dependence between memory-accessing components of the two decisions

span.label: **THE FIRST MEASUREMENT OF THE EFFECT, WITH ITS ERROR BAR:** `"Yes" responses averaged 85 ± 19 msec, faster for pairs of ASSOCIATED words than for pairs of UNASSOCIATED words, F (1, 11) = 20.6, p < .001.` Two strings shown at once, one above the other, decide whether both are words. **There is no prime and no target** - the design is simultaneous and symmetric, which is worth holding onto, because everything downstream assumes a sequence and an asymmetry that this experiment did not have
span.quote: "Yes" responses averaged 85 ± 19 msec, faster for pairs of associated words than for pairs of unassociated words, F (1, 11) = 20.6, p < .001

span.label: **AND THE PAPER DECLINES THE INFERENCE ITS OWN NAME WOULD LATER REST ON:** `The effect of association on RT DOES NOT NECESSARILY IMPLY THAT THE MEANING OF A WORD IS RETRIEVED to make a lexical decision.` The founding result of semantic priming, and its authors say in the discussion that it does not establish semantic retrieval. **The word `semantic` in `semantic priming` is a claim this sentence explicitly withholds** - and the withholding is not hedging, it is followed by a worked alternative in which association affects RT through the organisation of memory locations rather than through meaning
span.quote: The effect of association on RT does not necessarily imply that the meaning of a word is retrieved to make a lexical decision

span.label: **TWO MECHANISMS, NO TEST, AND THE PAPER SAYS SO RATHER THAN PICKING:** `The present data do not provide a direct test between this location-shifting model and the spreading-excitation model.` It then does something better than choosing - it asks what survives the choice: `REGARDLESS OF WHETHER spreading excitation, location shifting, comparison of meanings, or some other process is involved, the effects of association appear limited neither to semantic decisions nor to same-different judgments.` **The result is stated at the level the data supports and the mechanism is left open**, which is exactly what neely1977 spends 28 pages building an experiment to settle six years later
span.quote: Regardless of whether spreading excitation, location shifting, comparison of meanings, or some other process is involved, the effects of association appear limited neither to semantic decisions nor to same-different judgments

span.label: **AND THE LIMITATION IS STATED IN ONE FLAT SENTENCE WITH NO SOFTENING:** `At present we do not have ways to test all the possible explanations of these effects.` No `future work will`, no `it remains to be seen`. **This corpus has 539 records and I have read few limitation sentences this short** - and it belongs to the paper that started the literature, which is the opposite of the order one would expect confidence to arrive in
span.quote: At present we do not have ways to test all the possible explanations of these effects

span.label: contradicts → Schaeffer and Wallace (1969, 1970)
span.quote: Our reasoning suggests, furthermore, that the findings of Schaeffer and Wallace (1969, 1970) may not have resulted solely from a comparison of word meanings

span.label: builds-on → Meyer (1971)
span.quote: Recently, Meyer (1971) has collected data in other tasks that are consistent with this notion

span.label: dependence —operationalised-as→ association
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.95 — **THE WHOLE DESIGN IN ONE SENTENCE, AND IT IS AN OPERATIONALISATION NOT A FINDING.** `BY VARYING the degree of association between the words, we then HOPED IT WOULD BE POSSIBLE TO TEST FOR a dependence between memory-accessing components of the two decisions.` The dependence is the thing wanted; association is the handle built to reach it. Weight 0.95 - the sentence is explicit, both endpoints are named, and the direction is unambiguous because `test for` only reads one way. The `hoped` is theirs and I have kept it in the quote: at the point this sentence is written the design is a bet, not a result.
span.quote: By varying the degree of association between the words, we then hoped it would be possible to test for a dependence between memory-accessing components of the two decisions

span.label: spreading excitation —distinct-from→ location shifting
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.85 — **THE EDGE IS CARRIED BY A LIST, WHICH IS WHY IT IS 0.85 AND NOT HIGHER.** The sentence that draws the contrast explicitly - `the present data do not provide a direct test between this LOCATION-SHIFTING model and the SPREADING-EXCITATION model` - writes both names hyphenated, and the concept nodes are the unhyphenated forms. So the triple is built from the sentence that lists them as alternatives instead. **Distinctness is genuinely asserted there** - `regardless of whether X, Y, Z, or some other process` only makes sense if they are different processes - but it is asserted in passing, on the way to saying the effect survives the question. The stronger sentence exists; a hyphen keeps it out, exactly as a plural kept the logogen edge out of neely1977 an hour ago. **Two edges lost to orthography in one evening** is worth recording as a pattern rather than as two accidents.
span.quote: Regardless of whether spreading excitation, location shifting, comparison of meanings, or some other process is involved, the effects of association appear limited neither to semantic decisions nor to same-different judgments
